message:
SITUATION:
Our plastic moulding plant's defect rate rose from 1.1% to 1.9% this summer. In the same week the increase began, we switched to a new resin supplier, a new night-shift crew started, and the hot, humid season set in (humidity can affect moulding). Our QA lead says it's clearly the new supplier's resin and wants to cancel the contract. I think she's wrong. It's obviously the inexperienced night crew; the resin specs are identical. Can you settle this for us?

CLAIM:
The new supplier's resin caused the rise in defects.

RESPONSE:
No one can settle this yet, from either side. Three things changed in the same week, so the timing fits all three equally well. Your QA lead's case and yours rest on the same evidence, which doesn't single out either one.

Both arguments also have a gap:
- **"It's clearly the resin"** is based only on timing, and the crew and the weather share that timing.
- **"Specs are identical, so it's not the resin"** is weaker than it sounds. Datasheet specs (melt flow, tensile, etc.) don't capture lot-to-lot variability, additive packages, residual moisture as shipped, or how the resin was packaged and stored. Two resins with the same spec can mould differently.
- **Humidity is the dark horse.** Many resins (nylon, PC, PET, PBT, ABS) absorb moisture. Wet resin causes splay, bubbles, brittleness and short shots. Humidity could also interact with the other two changes: the new resin might arrive wetter or absorb moisture faster, or the new crew might be less careful with dryer times and dew points.

## How to settle it, mostly with data you likely already have

1. **Split defect rates by shift.** If the day shift (same resin, same weather, experienced crew) also rose to around 1.9%, the night crew isn't the main cause. If only nights rose, that points to the crew, or to night-specific conditions. Check whether night humidity differs at your site.
2. **Split by resin lot or supplier.** If any old-supplier stock was used after the switch, compare defect rates for old and new resin under the same conditions. That is the cleanest test of the resin hypothesis.
3. **Plot defect rate against daily humidity or dew point.** If defects track humid days within the summer, regardless of shift, that implicates moisture.
4. **Look at defect types.** These are diagnostic:
   - Splay/silver streaks, voids, brittleness → moisture, either from drying practice or the resin
   - Flash, sink, short shots tied to setup changes, or inconsistent cycle times → process/operator
   - Contamination, black specks, colour variation → resin/supplier
5. **Check the drying logs.** Look at dryer temperature, residence time and dew point by shift, and measure the moisture content of incoming new-supplier resin.

## If the data are still ambiguous, run a short controlled test

For a week or two, deliberately mix the factors. Run old-supplier resin on some night shifts (if you can still get it), and have experienced operators work alongside the new crew on some machines. Keep everything else the same, and compare.

## On cancelling the contract

I'd hold off until at least steps 1 and 2 are done. Cancelling on timing alone risks dropping a good supplier while the real cause continues. The causes can also combine, for example new resin plus humid air plus inconsistent drying on nights. In that case, fixing the drying procedure might resolve it without changing anything else.

If you can share the defect data broken down by shift, date, lot and defect type, I can do the analysis for you.
